PPT: Communication with Difficult Patients
text: Communication With Difficult Patients Done by: SARA ATTIA GHITANI Lecturer of Forensic Medicine & Clinical Toxicology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Learning Objectives Identify difficult patients. Enumerate common triggers that make a patient “difficult” Summarize issues of dealing with difficult patients. Enact strategies for working with difficult patients. Define Motivational Interviewing (MI) Convey the spirit and principles of MI The ideal patient suffers from an acute, treatable illness and becomes grateful when returned to good health. Any deviation by the patient from this model give a difficult patient who may elicit negative reactions from the physician. Some patients have behaviors that make interactions unpleasant, leading to suboptimal outcomes and physician burnout. 3 Difficult patient Definition: Those patients who elicit strong negative emotions from their physicians. If not acknowledged and managed correctly, these feelings can lead to diagnostic errors, unpleasant confrontations, and troublesome complaints or legal claims. What makes a patient “difficult”? What makes a patient “difficult”? 1. Demanding behaviors: Dependent clingers: those who have an inexhaustible need for love and attention. Manipulative Help-Rejectors: they are pessimistic and have little hope of recovery. These people need and crave attention, yet also fear their need for it. This leads to contradictory behaviour (patients who slash their own wrists, go to hospital, then refuse repair). that necessitate setting realistic limits to the doctor-patient relationship as 6 What makes a patient “difficult”? 2. Stay sick behaviors Worried Well Ignoring problems up to self-destructing deny Noncompliant undermine therapy Resistance to change as resisting lifestyle modifications in diabetic patients. 7 What makes a patient “difficult”? 4. Multiple complaints/ problems 5. Difficult diagnosis 8 What makes a patient “difficult”? Chronic pain Drug problems as drug seeking behaviour. 7. Psychiatric concerns as borderline PD, substance use disorders and bipolar disorder. 9 What makes a patient “difficult”? 8. Others as unfocused patients and slow talkers impeding communication. 10 What makes a patient “difficult”? 9. Every patient can become an “expert” via the Internet 11 When a patient becomes defensive after their internet-sourced information is challenged, the physician should: a) Stand firm and assert the inaccuracies of the information b) Listen empathetically and acknowledge their effort in seeking information c) Change the subject to avoid conflict d) Refer the patient to another doctor B ISSUES OF DEALING WITH DIFFICULT PATIENTS 1.Doctor-patient relationship- Rapport: Dealing with difficult patients can lead physicians to get out of control, this makes the patient get more and more frustrated. The battle becomes more important than the outcome. Saving face becomes a high priority before solving the problem. Rapport is a harmonious condition in which communication between doctor and patient is effective, and a feeling of mutual understanding exists. 14 2.Diagnostic Considerations The priority is always to diagnose or to exclude serious conditions. If there is no organic ailment and no intoxication, major psychiatric illness must be considered. • Do not allow your emotions to obscure your judgement. • You should not pass a difficult patient on to a consultant merely as a form of avoidance, but if you've made an honest assessment and still harbor diagnostic doubts, refer. 3.Legal Considerations Difficult patients may be angry and follow their encounter with complaint or lawsuits. convince the competent patient to stay until the assessment is complete. Patient wants to leave AMA, the patient should sign a release form that is witnessed. If the patient refuses to sign a release document, note this refusal on the chart. "Substituted consent" by a relative is valid only if the patient is incompetent, and the relative clearly acts in the patient's best interest. Patients are competent to consent or refuse consent if they can fully understand the nature of their problem and the risks or benefits of accepting or rejecting treatment. 16 Challenging Emotional Conversations with Patients & Families Challenging interview with difficult patients BUSTER protocol Motivational interview 1. BUSTER protocol • Be prepared • Use non-judgmental listening • Six second rule • Tell me more statements • Empathize and validate • Respond with a wish statement It is used to minimize emotions, so they don’t rule the conversation. 19 1. Be Prepared • Expect emotions. • Stay calm. • Plan for how you will deal. • Monitor what you think and feel • Practice self-regulation. • Turn the confrontation to conversation. • Know when NOT to have conversation (when emotions are too intense). 2. Use Non-Judgmental Listening Remember it’s not about you, but about the other’s disappointments, fears, anxiety and expectations which often underlie the anger, blame or denial on the surface. Maintain eye contact. Listen without interrupting, use clarifying statements or paraphrasing. Avoid trying to make a situation better when it is grave as saying, “I’m sure things will not be as bad as you think.” 3. Six Second Rule: Avoid escalation of conversation Well, it didn’t work because you waited too long to get help When your own emotions start to boil in response to anger, wait at least 6 seconds or more to calm down. • Avoid being defensive/blaming e.g. “.” • Gather your thoughts and use skills such as “tell me more” or empathic/validating responses. 22 4. Tell me more Tell me more about your husband. What happened after that? 23 5. Empathizing and validating to: I can see you weren’t expecting this It’s very stressful, isn’t it? It must be hard to come here every week I can see how difficult it is for you 24 AVOID I know how you feel. I feel your pain. It’s going to be alright. When your own emotions start to boil in response to anger, wait at least 6 seconds or more to calm down. • Avoid being defensive/blaming e.g. “.” • Gather your thoughts and use skills such as “tell me more” or empathic/validating responses. 25 6. Respond with a wish statement: I wish I didn’t have to tell you this…” I wish we had a more effective treatment Let the other person know you hear them and acknowledge that the goal may be desirable, but “I wish things had worked out better.” 26 How to deal in the following scenarios? Angry patient 1. Remain calm 2. Verbally comment on what you have observed I see you're angry; can we talk about it? I would be upset in your situation, but let's focus on how I can help you You entered the room, and the patient appears impatient Apologize for the delay while introducing yourself Sit or stand level with the patient, Make eye contact often, and try not to appear rushed If tests are required, give realistic estimates of how long they will take You feel yourself becoming angry or frustrated Do not deny your feelings, Honesty and sincerity will usually be rewarded. Find an excuse to leave the bedside for a few minutes before saying something you may regret later. I'm doing my best, but nothing seems to satisfy you try to identify what caused your reaction and formulate a strategy. 30 You feel yourself threatened/unsafe End the interaction This conversation is making me feel uncomfortable right now. I don’t feel safe right now and can’t continue this conversation.” 31 Switch strategies Sometimes you need to take command, other times, to compromise. Occasionally humor helps (be careful that you are not misunderstood) Never use excuses with difficult patients to escape Don’t escape by saying "I'm too busy," or "There are no beds." 34 Case Scenario: Ms. Lee arrives at the clinic visibly upset and complains about a long wait time for her appointment. She raises her voice and demands immediate attention, making the waiting room tense. The main issue: Angry Patient What should the healthcare provider's initial response be to Ms. Lee's anger? A) Respond with equal frustration and explain the busy schedule. B) Apologize for the wait and acknowledge her frustration. C) Ignore her complaints and proceed with the medical consultation. D) Ask her to leave if she cannot calm down. B The main issue: Angry Patient How can the healthcare provider effectively de-escalate the situation with Ms. Lee? A) Remain silent and let her vent without interruption. B) Tell her to calm down and wait her turn. C) Listen actively, validate her feelings, and provide a solution. D) Suggest she finds another clinic if she is dissatisfied. C Case Scenario Mr. Brown demands an unnecessary MRI scan. He read about its diagnostic value on the internet. Now, he is believing that it is the only way to diagnose his minor back pain despite the physician's recommendation for a more conservative approach. Expert patient through the Internet How should the physician address Mr. Brown's demand for an unnecessary MRI? A) Order the MRI to avoid conflict. B) Dismiss his concerns and refuse to discuss it further. C) Explain the rationale for the recommended approach and the risks of unnecessary tests. D) Refer him to another physician who might comply with his request. C Expert patient through the Internet What is an appropriate way to ensure Mr. Brown feels heard while maintaining professional integrity? A) Agree with everything Mr. Brown says to keep him satisfied. B) Provide detailed explanations and engage him in shared decision-making. C) Avoid discussing his concerns and focus on other health issues. D) Give in to his demands to avoid potential complaints. B 2. Motivational interview (MI) Definition: MI is a collaborative patient-centered directive method for enhancing intrinsic motivation to change by exploring and resolving ambivalence. Ambivalence • A state of mind in which a person has coexisting conflicting feelings, thoughts, and actions about a particular behavior. • Ambivalence maintains the gap between what people know and what they do. I should ---- BUT It is often marked by language such as a “but” in the middle as “I should change, but --- 42 Ambivalence • Interpreting ambivalence as denial, carelessness or resistance increases friction between you and your patient. • Ambivalence is normal and does not mean that a person is unmotivated. • It is important to understand and accept your patient's ambivalence because ambivalence is often the central problem. I should ---- BUT Ambivalence maintains the gap between what people know and what they do. It is often marked by language such as a “but” in the middle as “I should change, but --- 43 Goal of MI: The goal of MI is to help people see discrepancies between their present behaviors and broader goals through the identification, examination, and resolution of ambivalence about changing behavior. Thus, it is of value with difficult patient who resist to change and non-compliant with therapy. Spirit of MI is based on Collaboration Autonomy Evocation Spirit of MI is based on: Collaboration – MI rests on a collaborative partnership. Instead of directing the passive patient in what to do, there is an active collaborative conversation and joint decision-making process. This is particularly vital in health behavior change, because ultimately only the patient can make the change. Spirit of MI is based on: b. Evocation – listening and eliciting MI evoke from patients what they already have and activate their own motivations for change through connecting health behavior change with what patients care about, with their own values and concerns. 1) Where are you right now in …… ? 2)Where would you like to be? 3)What is currently preventing this happening? Spirit of MI is based on: c. Autonomy – Decision making is left to the patient Practitioners may inform, advise, even warn, but ultimately it is the patient who decides what to do. Autonomy is key in facilitating lasting change. There is something inherent in human nature that resists being coerced and told what to do. So, it is the professional’s responsibility to respect the patient’s ability to choose and accept that people make choices for themselves. 48 Principles of MI: 1. Resisting the righting reflex – • A patient’s response to the righting reflex is feeling not heard, not-understood, helpless, trapped and oppositional. • So instead, allow patients to explore both sides of their ambivalence to able to give reasons for change. Principles of MI: 2. Understand and explore the patient’s motivation- What is it that they want?/ Exploring DARN: Desire – Determine the patients desire to change (when desire is low, this is a signal to move back to following – reflect the resistance) Ability – How does the patient see her ability to change? (Ruler – From 1-10 with one being completely unable and ten being completely able, where do you see your ability?) Reasons –why they should change? (Pros vs. Cons) Need – why they need to change? 50 Principles of MI: 3. Listen with empathy Acceptance facilitates change. Skillful reflective listening is fundamental. Remember ambivalence is expected and normal Desire – Determine the patients desire to change (when desire is low, this is a signal to move back to following – reflect the resistance) Ability – How does the patient see her ability to change? (Ruler – From 1-10 with one being completely unable and ten being completely able, where do you see your ability?) Reasons –why they should change? (Pros vs. Cons) Need – why they need to change? 51 Principles of MI: 4. Empower – support self-efficacy- encouraging hope and optimism Once the patient has expressed his own desire to change, told you their confidence in being able to make the change, and told you reasons - then it is time to start taking steps to change. An example of a good directing style is using an Elicit-Provide-Elicit  Elicit - Can I tell you more about how to ..-Would you like me to tell you more about….  Provide – Give information  Elicit – Is there anything else on …. 52 Motivational good directive style MI Communication Styles: MI starts with a 1) listening 2) guiding (exploring options). 3) directive (giving advice). If you move into directing too soon, the chances for behavior change go down considerably. OARS is a brief way to remember the basic approach used in Motivational Interviewing Open Ended Questions: we ask questions the answer to which is change talk, we want the person talk about change. Affirmations: emphasizing patient’s past experiences that demonstrate strength, success, or power can prevent discouragement. Reflections: Helping people to say their arguments and then hearing them back makes them more familiar with what they believe. Summaries: Summaries reinforce what has been said, show that you have been listening carefully, and prepare to move on. 55 Case Scenario Dr. Smith is treating Mr. Johnson, a patient with diabetes. Despite repeated advice, Mr. Johnson continues to neglect his medication and dietary restrictions, leading to uncontrolled blood sugar levels. Dr. Smith is frustrated but needs to find an effective way to communicate the importance of adherence to the treatment plan. The main issue: Non-compliant patient What is the most ethical approach for Dr. Smith to take in discussing Mr. Johnson's non-compliance? A) Scold Mr. Johnson for not following the treatment plan. B) Express understanding of the challenges and explore the reasons for non-compliance. C) Threaten to discontinue care if Mr. Johnson does not adhere to the treatment plan. D) Ignore the issue and continue prescribing medication as usual. B Case Scenario Mr. Brown demands an unnecessary MRI scan. He read about its diagnostic value on the internet. Now, he is believing that it is the only way to diagnose his minor back pain despite the physician's recommendation for a more conservative approach. Expert patient through the Internet How should the physician address Mr. Brown's demand for an unnecessary MRI? A) Order the MRI to avoid conflict. B) Dismiss his concerns and refuse to discuss it further. C) Explain the rationale for the recommended approach and the risks of unnecessary tests. D) Refer him to another physician who might comply with his request. C Expert patient through the Internet What is an appropriate way to ensure Mr. Brown feels heard while maintaining professional integrity? A) Agree with everything Mr. Brown says to keep him satisfied. B) Provide detailed explanations and engage him in shared decision-making. C) Avoid discussing his concerns and focus on other health issues. D) Give in to his demands to avoid potential complaints. B Case Scenario Ms. Patel has a history of medical anxiety and expresses distrust in the proposed treatment plan, fearing potential side effects and questioning the necessity of the intervention. The Distrustful Patient How can the healthcare provider address Ms. Patel's medical anxiety effectively? A) Ignore her anxiety and focus solely on the medical facts. B) Suggest she seek psychiatric help and avoid discussing her fears. C) Incorporate strategies like motivational interviewing to explore her concerns and support her. D) Reassure her without providing detailed explanations to save time. C
